list.listitem: The cardinal physical signs and symptoms of Parkinson disease (PD) are distal resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability. C
Levodopa (L-dopa) is the primary treatment, but its long-term use is limited by motor complications and drug-induced dyskinesias. A

Dopamine agonists are an option in conjunction with low-dose L-dopa for initial treatment of PD and have been shown to delay the onset of motor complications; however, dopamine agonists alone are inferior to L-dopa in controlling motor symptoms. A

In advanced PD, once L-dopa-related motor complications have developed, adjuvant therapy with dopamine agonists, catecholamine O-methyl transferase (COMT) inhibitors, or monoamine oxidase-B (MAO-B) inhibitors is beneficial.A
Treatment of non-motor symptoms such as depression, sialorrhea, and psychosis is essential. C
Deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus or globus pallidus pars interna can ameliorate symptoms in patients with advanced PD.A

background.definition: PD is a neurodegenerative disease with early prominent death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta leading to a movement disorder characterised by classical parkinsonian motor symptoms (resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural and gait impairment) as well as numerous non-motor symptoms.

list.listitem: The overall incidence rate is 17 per 100,000 person-years. The incidence of PD may have increased between 1976 and 2005, particularly in men 70 years and older.
The overall prevalence of PD in North America among those aged ≥45 years is estimated to be 572 per 100,000.
The prevalence of PD has risen sharply over last two recent decades.
The estimated total annual cost in the United States is approximately $23 billion.
PD is caused by a combination of genetic and suspected environmental factors (eg, viruses, toxins, 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine, and well water).
The parkin gene located on chromosome 6q25.2-q27 has been linked to PD in families with young-onset PD.
Multiple genetic factors, including the tau gene on chromosome 17q21, have been implicated in idiopathic late-onset PD.
Patients with renal failure are at increased risk of Parkinsonism.
The retinal age gap is associated with the future risk of incident PD.
The pathologic hallmark of PD is loss of dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta.
This leads to decreased production of dopamine over time.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Living in rural areas, drinking well water, being exposed to pesticides, or working in a wood pulp mill

list.listitem: Four cardinal signs of PD are resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability.
Consider alternate diagnoses in patients without tremor, with significant dysautonomia, with rapid progression, with falls early in disease course, and poor response to L-dopa C
Imaging is not recommended unless another condition is suspected. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Preceding use of culprit medicines like antipsychotics, reserpine, or reglan; tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, often bilateral symptoms; normal radiologic findings

Stepwise progression; history of cerebrovascular accident/transient ischemic attack (CVA/TIA); comorbid cardiovascular diseases; fixed deficits from previous events; lesions in white matter and/or basal ganglia on CT or MRI

Frequent family history; little evolution; tremor often action based; absence of extrapyramidal symptoms (except possible mild rigidity); no response to L-dopa; tremor often bilateral with attenuation with alcohol; single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) reveals normal dopaminergic system
Ataxia, dementia, urinary incontinence; ataxic gait; mental status changes; hydrocephalus on CT or MRI

Progressive; onset after 40 years of age; vertical gaze paralysis (or slowed vertical saccadic movements); marked postural instability (falls within first year of disease); resting tremor is rare; nuchal dystonia; normal olfaction; MRI findings of mesencephalo-brainstem atrophy involving the superior colliculi

Differential.Differential_Name: Multiple system atrophy (MSA) including Shy-Drager syndrome, olivopontocerebellar atrophy, nigrostriatal degeneration
Differential.Differential_Features: Autonomic and urinary dysfunction; Parkinsonism with poor levodopa response; cerebellar dysfunction; documented autonomic dysfunction; a few patients have resting tremor; 25% have transient response to levodopa; MRI findings of nigrostriatal degeneration with gliosis in the lateral putamen with hyperintense proton density bands and hypointense bands in the T2 images

History of cortical and cognitive impairment with involuntary movements; apraxia, aphasia, sensory disorders, positive Babinski sign; asymmetric Parkinsonism without impaired deambulation; myoclonus, dystonia
Cognitive impairment, hallucinations, episodes of delirium, Parkinsonism; impaired attention and visuospatial abilities, falls, episodes of syncope; low glucose metabolism by PET in cortex

list.listitem: The Movement Disorder Society (MDS) defines the essential clinical diagnostic Criteria for PD.

The MDS criteria defines parkinsonism as bradykinesia, in combination with either rest tremor, rigidity, or both. Once parkinsonism has been diagnosed, diagnosis of Clinically Established PD requires: 1. Absence of absolute exclusion criteria 2. At least two supportive criteria, and 3. No red flags. Diagnosis of Clinically Probable PD requires: 1. Absence of absolute exclusion criteria 2. Presence of red flags counterbalanced by supportive criteria. If 1 red flag is present, there must also be at least 1 supportive criterion. If 2 red flags, at least 2 supportive criteria are needed. No more than 2 red flags are allowed for this category.
Three cardinal signs of PD are resting tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia.
Additional common findings are postural instability, typically a late finding in PD, asymmetric onset of symptoms, and symptomatic response to L-dopa (levodopa).
A history of falls actually makes the diagnosis less likely in patients with suspected PD.
The gold standard for diagnosis of PD is clinical criteria. Ancillary tests should be reserved for people presenting with an atypical presentation.
Although CT and MRI of the head show no specific patterns in patients with PD, they are often used to rule out or confirm other diseases when clinically suspected.

Dopaminergic neuroimaging identifies degeneration of the nigrostriatal system and therefore establishes parkinsonism although it is not recommended for routine use. It is particularly helpful in distinguishing dystonic tremor, essential tremor, functional overlay, drug-induced parkinsonism, or vascular parkinsonism from PD.

Genetic testing can establish a definitive diagnosis in selected cases of PD although it is not recommended for routine use. This information can be useful for family counseling and personalized treatment.

A DaT scan (Dopamine Transporter Scan) is a specialized imaging test that uses single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) to assess dopamine function in the brain. It is helpful in distinguishing parkinsonian syndromes associated with nigrostriatal degeneration from essential tremor. However, it cannot differentiate PD from other parkinsonian syndromes as both show reduced DAT uptake.

Diagnosis is primarily clinical. Consider an alternate diagnosis in patients without tremor, with significant dysautonomia, with rapid progression, falls early in disease course, and poor response to L-dopa.
Diagnostic testing (L-dopa challenge, olfactory testing, imaging studies) are primarily helpful when the diagnosis is in doubt and are not routinely recommended for all patients.
See for an overview of the approach to diagnosis and treatment of suspected PD.
Use L-dopa and dopamine agonists either as monotherapies or as adjuvant therapies for managing early stage PD. A
Treat motor complications by adding a dopamine agonist, a MAO-B inhibitor, or a COMT inhibitor. A

Be alert for the presence of non-motor symptoms such as depression, dementia, and psychosis and treat accordingly. Recommend speech and language therapy, physical therapy, and occupational therapy as appropriate.C
Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the subthalamic nucleus or globus pallidus pars interna can improve motor symptoms in patients with advanced PD.B
No therapy has been shown to slow the progression of PD.

Start symptomatic therapy when a patient becomes functionally impaired. Drugs used for the treatment of PD are summarized in , and an approach to initial therapy is given in . Guidelines from the Movement Disorder Society recommend non-ergotamine dopamine agonists, L-dopa, selegeline, and rasagaline as options for monotherapy. It may then progress to combination therapy as motor symptoms progress to include the MAO inhibitor rasagiline, a dopamine agonist, and low-dose L-dopa. COMT inhibitors are added later as motor fluctuations develop, and amantadine with the onset of dyskinesias.

L-dopa is the most effective pharmacologic agent for PD. One RCT of 361 patients with early PD compared three different doses (150 mg/d, 300 mg/d, and 600 mg/d) of L-dopa with placebo. The study found that L-dopa reduced the deterioration in unified PD rating scale (UPDRS) scores compared with placebo at 42 weeks. The combination of bromocriptine and levodopa is no better than bromocriptine alone.
Early treatment with levodopa in early PD relieves symptoms compared with delay-start but did not alter the disease course.

AAN guidelines (2021) note that in patients with early PD, initiating treatment with levodopa provides superior motor benefit compared to treatment with dopamine agonists. At the same time, levodopa is more likely than dopamine agonists to cause dyskinesia. There was little evidence that any one formulation was better than any other. In addition, levodopa with entacapone and long-acting forms of levodopa do not provide greater efficacy over immediate release version. Dopamine agonists are associated with a higher likelihood of impulse control disorders.

Lixisenatide is a GLP-1 agonist with possible neuroprotective properties. A trial randomized 156 persons with early (< 3 years diagnosed) Parkinson Disease to lixisenatide or placebo. After 1 year pogression of motor disability was slightly slower with lixisenatide (3 points on the 132 point scale). Adverse events were primarily gastrointestinal.
The MAOB inhibitors reduce disability, the need for levodopa, and the incidence of motor fluctuations, when given in early PD, without significant side effects or increased mortality.

Studies have demonstrated that dopamine agonists, alone or in combination with L-dopa, reduced the incidence of dyskinesias and motor complications compared with L-dopa alone. However, monotherapy with a dopamine agonist was associated with greater motor impairment and disability than L-dopa monotherapy.

When dopaminergic treatment is required, L-dopa or a dopamine agonist can be initiated depending on the need to improve motor disability (L-dopa is better) or the desire to minimize the risk of motor complications (dopamine agonists cause fewer motor complications). There is no difference between short- and long-acting L-dopa in effectiveness or long-term outcomes.
Gene therapies have been experimented but none of them have received regulatory approval.

Advances in developmental and stem cell biology have enabled the creation of cell-replacement therapies using dopamine neurons derived from human pluripotent stem cells, offering several advantages over therapies based on fetal cells.

Long-term therapy with L-dopa is often complicated by motor fluctuations and dyskinesia. Patients may experience a "wearing-off" effect characterized by a shorter duration of benefit from each L-dopa dose, causing Parkinsonian symptoms to reemerge. Patients can also experience an "on-off" effect characterized by unpredictable, abrupt fluctuations in motor state from when the medication is effective and symptoms are controlled ("on") to when parkinsonian symptoms worsen ("off").

Levodopa/carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) improved "off" time and quality of life in Parkinson's disease (PD) patients by reducing fluctuations in dopaminergic drug levels, thereby minimizing motor fluctuations. LCIG is infused continuously (up to 16 hours daily) through a percutaneous gastrostomy tube connected to a battery-powered pump. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has recently approved continuous subcutaneous infusion (CSI) of foslevodopa-foscarbidopa to manage motor fluctuations in advanced Parkinson's disease. It serves as an alternative to LCIG, which requires the placement of a gastrostomy tube. Both LCIG and CSI of foslevodopa-foscarbidopa may be suitable for patients who are too frail for deep brain stimulation (DBS).

Evidence-based guidelines from the Movement Disorder Society (2018) conclude that pramipexole, ropinorole, cabergoline, and pergolide are efficacious or likely efficacious for preventing or delaying the onset of dyskinesias. The same guidelines conclude that pramipexole and cabergoline are efficacious for preventing or delaying the onset of motor fluctuations. Dopamine agonists pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine, and apomorphine are efficacious for treatment of motor fluctuations, as are pergolide, COMT inhibitors, and MAO-B inhibitors. For treatment of dyskinesias, amantadine and clozapine are efficacious.
Patient-rated quality of life is inferior with COMT inhibitors as adjuvant treatment compared with MAO-B inhibitors or dopamine agonists among those with motor complications uncontrolled by levodopa.

Systematic reviews have demonstrated that dopamine agonists such as pramipexole and ropinirole may significantly reduce "off" time, improving motor impairment and disability and reducing the need for L-dopa. Both the immediate release and long-acting versions of pramipexole and ropinirole are effective. A Cochrane review concludes more data is needed to assess the benefit of ropinirole for L-dopa induced complications. COMT inhibitors (eg, entacapone [Comtan], tolcapone [Tasmar]) decrease the degradation of L-dopa and extend its half-life, thus relieving the end-of-dose wearing-off effect and reducing "off" time.
Bromocriptine, cabergoline, and ropinorole have similar effects in reducing "off" time and decreasing L-dopa dose.

Medium-term evidence indicates cabergoline modestly improves motor impairment and disability for the "wearing off" phenomena of L-Dopa. Other drugs to reduce "off" time include apomorphine, cabergoline (Dostinex), and selegiline (Eldepryl).

Lower supine plasma norepinephrine levels accurately identify patients with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (nOH) that are more likely to have a greater pressor effect from droxidopa. This finding helps identify patients with nOH who will most likely benefit from standard doses of droxidopa.
Isradipine, a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker, was shown to be ineffective to slow the progression of symptoms in early-stage PD in one small RCT.

Rivastigmine can improve gait stability as indicated by improved step time variability for normal walking and simple dual task, and potially reduce falls. The International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society concludes that it is likely efficacious and possibly usefule for treatment of gait and balance symptoms in PD.
Cholinesterase inhibitors may reduce the rate of falls, but it is unclear whether they have reduce the number of people falling.

Cholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil and rivastigmine improve global assessment, cognitive function, behavioral disturbance, and activities of daily living. Rivastigmine causes some adverse events.
Recommended medications for psychoses that will not worsen motor symptoms include clozapine, quetiapine, and pimavanserin.
Valproate preparations do not improve agitation in dmentia and there is concern for harmful effects.
The transcutaneous tibial nerve stimulation improves symptoms of bladder dysfunction associated with PD.
Caffeine does not appear to improve symptoms.

While iron content is increased in the substantia nigra of persons with PD, a randomized trial with 372 participants found that compared with placebo, use of deferiprone worsened symptoms over a 36 week period.
A randomized trial with 235 participants found no benefit of simvastatin 40 mg to 80 mg daily compared with placebo.

The monoclonal antibody prasinezumab targets aggregated alpha-synuclein. A randomized trial with 316 participants randomized them to placebo, prasinezumab 1500 mg once monthly, or 4500 mg once monthly for a year. There was no difference between groups in symptom or imaging outcomes.
A second monoclonal antibody that targets aggregated alpha-synuclein (cinpanemab) was also found to be infective in a randomized trial Phase 2 trial with 357 participants.

Nilotinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for treatment of chronic myeloid leukemia. In a randomized trial comparing 150 mg and 300 mg doses once daily with placebo, the 300 mg dose caused significantly worse scores in the Movement Disorder Society Unified PD Rating Scale.
A randomized trial with 298 patients with early PD found no benefit to using inosine as a way to slow progression. It increases the risk of nephrolithiasis.

The 2018 Movement Disorder Society guidelines recommend bilateral deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the subthalamic nucleus (STN), DBS of the globus pallidus pars interna (GPi), and thalidotomy as effective treatment for motor flucutations and dyskinesias.
A small RCT of 90 patients concluded that DBS of the STN was more effective than DBS of the GPi at improving motor symptoms.

A randomized trial with 44 patients in Florida compared standard care with DBS provided by a home health nurse in the participant's home. There was no difference in outcomes, although the study is limited by its small sample size.

Patients (n = 40) with very asymmetrical PD were randomized 2:1 to DBS with focused ultrasound of the subthalamic nucleus or a sham procedure. Those in the active group had a decrease in their MDS-UPDRS III score from 19.9 to 9.9 after 4 months, compared to 18.7 to 17.1 in the sham group (p <0.001). Patients receiving active therapy had adverse events including weakness, dyskinesia, and speech and gait disturbances.

A small RCT randomized 94 patients with PD and dyskinesias or motor fluctuations and motor impairment in a 3:1 ratio to unilateral ultrasound ablation of the internal segment of the globus pallidus or a sham procedure. While more patients clinically responded in the active treatment group, adverse events included facial weakness, dysarthria, gait disturbance, loss of taste, and visual disturbances.

A systematic review revealed that cannabis, cannabidiol (CBD), and nabilone (a synthetic form of THC) consistently demonstrated greater efficacy than placebo in alleviating motor symptoms. Additionally, all treatments showed benefits for various non-motor symptoms, with cannabis notably reducing pain intensity and CBD alleviating psychiatric symptoms in a dose-dependent manner.
Tai Chi is superior to stretching and resistance training to improve balance and gait and reduces the risk of falls.
Acupuncture, biofeedback, fava beans, manual therapy, cowhage or velvet beans, and the Alexander technique are of unproven benefit.
Co-enzyme Q10 is safe in PD and may improve function.
Vitamin E does not improve motor function.
A systematic review found moderate to high quality evidence for the efficacy of the cannabinoid dronabinol for PD, with low to moderate magnitude of benefit.
Exercise interventions probably reduce the rate of falls, and probably slightly reduce the number of people falling in people with mild to moderate PD.
Performing a selective corrective exercise on balance pad improves falling and functional balance.
Consider speech therapy for patients with PD and dysarthria, especially to improve speech volume. There is not enough data to support one form of speech and language therapy over another.
Cognitive training is safe and modestly effective in patients with mild to moderate PD.
Occupational therapy is widely recommended and is unlikely to be harmful.
Strong evidence regarding the value of occupational therapy, exercise and speech therapy are lacking, though.
Preliminary data indicates automated mechanical peripheral stimulation (AMPS) may be an effective add-on therapy for treating gait variability in patients with PD and freezing of gait.
Consider consulting a neurologist if there is uncertainty regarding the diagnosis.
Consult a PD specialist for managing advanced stage PD associated with significant motor disturbances and dyskinesias.
Consult a PD specialist for management of medication-related complications.
Consult a physical therapist, to provide treatment strategies for motor difficulties.
Consult speech therapists to address speech and swallowing disturbances.
Consider hospitalization for patients with infectious, neurologic, or psychiatric complications of PD when outpatient management has failed.

Depression: the AAN guidelines recommend the Beck Depression Inventory and Hamilton Depression Rating Scale to screen for depression in PD. The Geriatric Depression Scale is a simpler four-item screen that may be more practical at the point of care. SSRIs are preferred to tricyclics due to better side effect profiles. While amitriptyline has been effective in treatment of depression in patients with PD, it should not be first line due to anticholinergic and orthostatic side effects. A small RCT found that nortriptyline is more effective than paroxetine in depressed PD patients. Telephone-based cognitive behavioral therapy is an option for patients with depression.

Cognitive impairment: the Mini-Mental State Exam and the Cambridge Cognitive Examination (CAMCog) are useful screening tools for dementia in patients with PD. Search for and treat medical problems such as dehydration, metabolic disorders, or infections, adjust anti-parkinsonian medications, and decrease/discontinue anticholinergics, dopamine, amantadine, and selegiline. Consider a trial of a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil or rivastigmine). Only rivastigmine has been specifically studied in PD patients with dementia.

Sleep disturbance: (1) day-time somnolence and sleep attacks are usually due to dopamine agonist, so discontinue it; (2) night-time awakenings may be due to overnight bradykinesia, so consider a bed-time dose of long-acting L-dopa, adjuvant entacapone, or a dopamine agonist; (3) if rapid eye movement behavior disorder develops, reduce or discontinue night-time dose of anti-parkinsonian drugs.
Dysphagia: evaluate swallowing and refer to speech/swallowing specialist; increase "on" time and eat during "on" time.

Constipation: increase fluid, fiber, and bulk, increase physical activity, stop anticholinergics, and/or use stool softeners, lactulose, mild laxatives, or enemas as needed. Multistrain probiotics may improve bowel movement frequency and improve satisfaction with treatment compared to placebo, NNT = 3.
Urinary urgency: reduce evening fluid intake; consider tolterodine or oxybutynin; and consider referral for urology evaluation if needed.
Orthostatic hypotension: eliminate antihypertensive medication; elevate head of bed; rise slowly from a prone position; and consider the use of fludrocortisone or midodrine.
Almost all patients respond to treatment with carbidopa/L-dopa; however, disabling motor complications often occur within 5 to 10 years. B
PD is associated with increased mortality; RR of death compared with matched control populations ranges from 1.6 to 3.0. B
PD is progressive and is currently incurable.
Dementia is common in patients with PD, and in one study was present within 5 years in 40% of men and 25% of women with PD over 70 years of age.
PD is progressive and is currently incurable. Although patients respond initially to treatment with carbidopa/L-dopa, disabling motor complications often occur with in 5 to 10 years.
In a cohort study, 130 people with PD were treated and followed for 10 years. At 10 years, 25% had been admitted to a nursing home. The mean duration of disease until death was 9.1 years.
PD is associated with increased mortality; RR of death compared with matched control populations ranges from 1.6 to 3.0. A
Schedule periodic follow-up visits to evaluate motor difficulties, neuropsychiatric disorders, and sleep difficulties and to adjust medications.
The UPDRS is a standardized assessment tool that facilitates documentation of disease progression and treatment response. Consider updating it annually.
Most patients should be seen every 3 to 6 months.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend the use of biomarkers in monitoring PD progression.

Avoid drugs known to induce PD, including older "typical" antpsychotics such as haloperidol and chlorpromazine; also avoid drugs to control nausea such as prochlorperazine, and drugs for GI motility disorders such as metoclopramide.
Advise patients with decreased L-dopa response to restrict dietary protein.
Inform patients regarding support groups and educational materials.

cell.label: Patient presents with signs and symptoms consistent with parkinsonism. Idiopathic Parkinson's disease confirmed based on clinical exam?
Consider immediate-release carbidopa/L-dopa (Sinemet) or a dopamine agonist.
Consider referral for apomorphine (Apokyn) therapy. If no improvement, refer for possible neurosurgery.
If severe dyskinesia, reduce carbidopa/levodopa (L-dopa) dose; if patient is taking controlled-release preparation, change to immediate-release; consider amantadine (Symmetrel).
If no improvement, refer for possible neurosurgery.

If motor complications, fractionate carbidopa/L-dopa therapy five times, a day, and consider adding a dopamine agonist, MAO-B inhibitor, or COMT inhibitor. If severe, consider referral for apomorphine (Apokyn) therapy.
If disease progresses, increase immediate-release carbidopa/L-dopa dose or increase dopamine agonist to the maximum tolerated dose and then add carbidopa/levodopa.
Consider CT or MRI to rule out normal pressure hydrocephalus or a vascular cause; consider referral to a subspecialist.

footnotes.footnote: Abbreviations: COMT, catechol O-methyltransferase; MAO-B, monoamine oxidase-B.

feature.caption: FDA-Approved Medications for Parkinson Disease (PD).
feature.feature_body:
Medication Adverse Effects Indications and Comments
Carbidopa/Levodopa (L-dopa)
Immediate- and sustained-release carbidopa/L-dopa (Sinemet) Nausea, somnolence, dyskinesia, hypotension, hallucinations L-dopa is the most effective medication and remains the primary treatment for symptomatic PD; no added benefit for motor complications with sustained-release versus immediate-release preparations. Initiating therapy in early stage disease with low doses of L-dopa and a dopamine agonist early in the course of the illness to delay onset of adverse effect. May also be used as monotherapy in early stages of disease.
COMT Inhibitors
Entacapone (Comtan) Diarrhea; exacerbates L-dopa adverse effects; bright orange urine COMT inhibitors are useful for managing motor fluctuations ("wearing-off" effect) in patients taking L-dopa; L-dopa dose may need to be reduced if dyskinesia appears
Tolcapone (Tasmar) Diarrhea; exacerbates L-dopa adverse effects; rare liver failure (liver function monitoring needed)
Dopamine Agonists
Ergot: bromocriptine, pergolide, cabergoline Nausea, headache, dizziness Useful for early and advanced disease. May be used as monotherapy in early stages of disease.
Non-ergot: pramipexole (Mirapex), ropinirole (Requip), rotigotine Nausea, sleep attacks, edema, hallucinations, hypotension Useful for early disease and in patients with PD and motor fluctuations. May be used as monotherapy in early stages of disease.
Monoamine Oxidase-B (MAO-B) Inhibitors
Rasagiline (Azilect) Weight loss, hypotension, dry mouth, drug interactions with other MAO inhibitors/tyramine Useful for symptomatic control of early stage PD (benefits are mild to moderate) and as adjuvant therapy for patients with PD and motor fluctuations
Selegiline (Eldepryl) Nausea, insomnia, drug interactions with other MAO inhibitors/tyramine
NMDA Receptor Inhibitor
Amantadine (Symmetrel) Nausea, hypotension, hallucinations, confusion, edema Useful for treating akinesia, rigidity, tremor, dyskinesia
Abbreviations: FDA, U.S. Food and Drug Administration; COMT, catechol O-methyltransferase; MAO-B, monoamine oxidase-B; NMDA, N-methyl-D-aspartate. From Rao SS, Hofmann LA, Shakil A. Parkinson's disease: diagnosis and treatment. Am Fam Physician 2006;74:2046-2054.
